topic: The Geometric Intuition of Cramer's Rule
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

outline.topic: The Geometric Intuition of Cramer's Rule
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: The Algebra-Geometry Bridge
sections.content: Introduce the standard system of two linear equations as a vector addition problem. Transition from the 'stack of equations' view to the 'vector combination' view: finding how much of vector A and vector B we need to reach a target vector W.
sections.example: A delivery drone (the target vector W) needs to reach a specific coordinate using two wind currents (vectors A and B) blowing in different directions.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Determinant as Area
sections.content: Briefly recap that the determinant of a 2x2 matrix represents the signed area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors. This is the 'base area' of our system.
sections.example: An animation showing two vectors (2,0) and (0,2) spanning a square with an area of 4, which is the determinant of the identity-like matrix.

sections.title: The Parallel-Transposition Trick
sections.content: Explain that the target vector W is composed of xA + yB. Visually demonstrate that if we form a parallelogram with W and B, the 'y' component of W disappears because it is parallel to B, leaving only the contribution of the 'x' component.
sections.example: Showing a parallelogram spanned by (xA + yB) and B. Since yB and B are on the same line, they contribute zero area. The area is purely determined by the 'x' scaling of vector A.

sections.title: The Ratio of Areas (Finding x)
sections.content: Show the core geometric proof of Cramer's Rule: The area of the parallelogram formed by (W, B) is exactly 'x' times the area of the parallelogram formed by (A, B). Therefore, x = Area(W, B) / Area(A, B).
sections.example: A visual split-screen: Left side shows the original area (A and B). Right side shows the modified area where A is replaced by W. A 'Scale Factor' label appears as the ratio between them.

sections.title: Symmetry for y and Higher Dimensions
sections.content: Apply the same logic to find 'y' by replacing the second column (vector B) with W. Briefly mention that in 3D, this moves from areas of parallelograms to volumes of parallelepipeds.
sections.example: The drone example again: To find the 'y' wind strength, we swap the 'B' current with our target destination and compare it to the original 'wind map' area.

sections.title: Summary and the 'Cramer Formula'
sections.content: Conclude by revealing the classic algebraic Cramer's formula as a direct result of these geometric area ratios. Emphasize why the determinant of the coefficient matrix cannot be zero (the area must exist).
sections.example: The final formula x = det(Ax)/det(A) and y = det(Ay)/det(A) appearing over the geometric shapes, showing they are one and the same.

storyboard.title: The Algebra-Geometry Bridge
lecture_lines: Linear systems can be seen as vector combinations.
We seek scalars x and y for vector W.
W equals x times A plus y times B.
This transforms algebra into a geometric puzzle.
We must find how to reach the target destination.
animations: Show the 2x2 system of equations in white #FFFFFF.
Transform the equations into the vector equation xA + yB = W.
Draw vectors A (#00FF00) and B (#0000FF) on a 2D grid.
Draw target vector W (#FF0000) representing the drone's goal.
Show scaled vectors xA and yB forming a tip-to-tail sum to W.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Determinant as Area
lecture_lines: The determinant represents the area of a parallelogram.
Vectors A and B form our system's base area.
This area is the determinant of matrix AB.
animations: Display vectors A (#00FF00) and B (#0000FF) starting from the origin.
Create a parallelogram with A and B and fill with #888888.
Label the area of this parallelogram as det(A, B) in white #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: The Parallel-Transposition Trick
lecture_lines: Consider the parallelogram formed by vectors W and B.
Since yB is parallel to B, its area is zero.
Only the xA component contributes to this new area.
animations: Plot W (#FF0000) and B (#0000FF) on the 2D grid.
Form a parallelogram using W and B with #FFAAAA fill.
Highlight the component of W parallel to B in yellow #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: The Ratio of Areas (Finding x)
lecture_lines: Replace vector A with target vector W.
The new area is x times the original area.
This geometric scaling reveals the value of x.
Thus, x is the ratio of these two areas.
This ratio is the essence of Cramer's Rule.
animations: Show Parallelogram(A, B) and Parallelogram(W, B) on a split screen.
Animate the transformation of Parallelogram(W, B) into Parallelogram(xA, B).
Scale Parallelogram(A, B) by x to match the area of Parallelogram(xA, B).
Display the ratio x = Area(W, B) / Area(A, B) in white #FFFFFF.
Reveal the determinant form x = det(W, B) / det(A, B) in white #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Symmetry for y and Higher Dimensions
lecture_lines: To find y, replace vector B with vector W.
The same area ratio logic applies to find y.
In 3D, we compare volumes of parallelepipeds instead.
animations: Replace B with W (#FF0000) in the original setup with A (#00FF00).
Display the formula y = det(A, W) / det(A, B) in white #FFFFFF.
Show a 3D volume (parallelepiped) briefly to generalize to 3D.

storyboard.title: Summary and the 'Cramer Formula'
lecture_lines: Cramer's Rule links geometric areas to algebraic solutions.
The solution exists if the base area is non-zero.
This formula works for any number of dimensions.
Algebra and geometry unite in this elegant solution.
Understanding this bridge simplifies complex linear systems.
animations: Present the general Cramer's Rule formula for xi in white #FFFFFF.
Flash the denominator det(A) in red #FF0000 to show singularity.
Final drone animation showing it reaching the target W using x and y.
Highlight the geometric-algebraic link with text 'Bridge'.
Fade out everything except the final formulas in white #FFFFFF.
